PA3605 Cosmology: additional material for Lecture 11

Matter-radiation equality

We saw in the last lecture that the photon density in the present-day Universe is Ωγ=2.47×10-5⁢h-2 (with the dependence on the Hubble parameter arising because the measured quantity is ρ rather than Ω). One can also show (beyond the scope of this course) that the neutrino density Ων=0.68⁢Ωγ, so the total radiation density111 Where “radiation” refers to all highly-relativistic particles. is given by

Ωr,0=4.15×10-5⁢h-2 (1)

From this point we can work backwards to find the entire thermal history of the Universe. We saw earlier that the matter and radiation densities scale as a-3 and a-4, respectively, so their early-time behaviour can be calculated directly from the present-day values:

ΩrΩm=Ωr,0⁢a-4Ωm,0⁢a-3=Ωr,0Ωm,0⁢1a (2)

Recall that decoupling occurred at z≃1100 (i.e., a≃1/1100). The radiation-to-matter density ratio at decoupling was therefore

ΩrΩm≃4.15×10-5Ωm,0⁢h2⁢11100≃0.3 (3)

where we have assumed Ωm,0=0.3 and h=0.7. Thus at decoupling there was ∼3 times more non-relativistic matter in the Universe than relativistic particles, and we thus say that the Universe at this point was matter-dominated. At even earlier times, however, this ratio increases, and we can find the point of so-called matter-radiation equality by requiring Ωr=Ωm, so that

aeq=Ωr,0Ωm,0≃124 000⁢Ωm,0⁢h2≃2.8×10-4 (4)

which corresponds to a redshift zeq≃3500. At earlier times (higher redshifts) than this the density of the Universe was dominated by relativistic particles.

The time-temperature relationship

To a good approximation we can assume that the Universe transitioned instantaneously from the radiation-dominated epoch to the matter-dominated epoch at zeq. We know how the scale-factor a behaves in each of these regimes, and since the temperature T∝a-1, this gives us enough information to calculate T over the full history of the Universe.

We first make the approximation that k=0 and Λ=0; while this may not be true in the present-day Universe, it’s clear from the scaling of the various components that both of these are negligible at early times. From zeq to z=0 the scale-factor therefore takes on the matter-dominated solution (which we derived in Lecture 6)

a∝t2/3 (5)

so during this epoch

T∝t-2/3 (6)

We fix the constant of proportionality by knowing the age of the Universe at z=0, so222 This is a slight fudge; Equation 7 assumes an age of 4×1017 s = 12.7 Gyr rather than the true age of 13.8 Gyr, to compensate for ignoring Λ in Equation 5.

T(t)=Tcmb(t4×1017⁢s)-2/3 ,t≥teq (7)

where Tcmb=2.725 K is the temperature of the present-day CMB. This relationship is valid in the matter-dominated epoch z<zeq, and we have

Teq=T⁢(zeq)=Tcmbaeq≃66 000⁢Ωm,0⁢h2⁢K≃9700⁢K (8)

with the last value calculated assuming Ωm,0=0.3 and h=0.7. The age of the Universe at matter-radiation equality is therefore

teq≃1.0×1011⁢Ωm,0-3/2⁢h-3⁢s=3400⁢Ωm,0-3/2⁢h-3⁢yr≃60 000⁢yr (9)

We saw above that decoupling occurred later than equality (with Tdec≃3000 K), so we can also apply Equation 7 to find the age of the Universe at decoupling

tdec≃380 000⁢yr (10)

At times earlier than teq (or temperatures higher than Teq) the Universe is radiation-dominated, and (again recalling Lecture 6) we have

a∝t1/2 (11)

so during this epoch

T∝t-1/2 (12)

We can set the constant of proportionality from the point of equality, or directly from the Friedmann equation333 See equation 11.12 of Liddle., and find (for z>zeq)

T(t)≃1.3×1010K(t1⁢s)-1/2 ,t≤teq (13)

or, equivalently

kBT≃1.1MeV(t1⁢s)-1/2 ,t≤teq (14)

These very high temperatures at early times in the expansion are why we use the term Hot Big Bang to describe our current understanding of the early Universe.

Primordial nucleosynthesis

The typical binding energies of atomic nuclei are ∼MeV. At higher temperatures than this thermal energy is sufficient to dissociate atomic nuclei, but as the Universe cools we eventually reach a point where nuclei remain bound444 One can alternatively think of this in terms of nuclear reactions. The “forward” reactions which form bound (light) nuclei are exothermic; the “reverse” reactions which destroy the nuclei are endothermic. When the temperature is high there is sufficient thermal energy to sustain the reverse reaction and so the system exists in equilibrium between formation and dissociation, but eventually the temperature drops to the point where only the forward reaction can proceed (usually until the supply of reactants is exhausted).. This is sometimes referred to as freeze-out, and we see from Equation 14 that the formation of the light elements via freeze-out is expected to happen when the Universe is around 1 s old. Knowing the temperature history of the Universe, and the relevant nuclear physics (binding energies and reaction rates), we can therefore calculate the formation of the light elements as the Universe cools. Here we will consider a simplified analysis to find the abundance of 24He (the dominant nucleus in the Universe after 1H).

Our analysis will make use of the temperature-time relationship derived above (Equation 14), some reaction energies (which we will simply quote as known results from nuclear physics), and three additional facts:

  1. i)

    Neutrons are slightly heavier than protons: mp=938.3 MeV/c2 and mn=939.6 MeV/c2. The mass difference Δ⁢m=mn-mp=1.3 MeV/c2.

  2. ii)

    Free neutrons decay, with a half-life t1/2=610 s (or equivalently an exponential decay time-scale tn=t1/2/log⁡2=880 s).

  3. iii)

    Neutrons in stable, bound nuclei do not decay.

We start our analysis at a time before nuclei have formed, but when the temperature is low enough that protons and neutrons are non-relativistic (i.e., kB⁢T≪mp⁢c2=938.3 MeV). The number density of both protons and neutrons therefore follows a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution555 In this lecture we will use the slightly unconventional upper-case N to denote number densities, to avoid confusion with the lower-case n which we are using for “neutron”., so

N∝m3/2⁢exp⁡(-m⁢c2kB⁢T) (15)

The constant of proportionality is the same for different species, so cancels out if we consider their ratios. The ratio of the neutron to proton number densities is therefore

NnNp=(mnmp)3/2⁢exp⁡(-Δ⁢m⁢c2kB⁢T) (16)

Free neutrons decay into protons (via beta decay); the reverse reaction which converts protons (and electrons) back into neutrons freezes out at kB⁢Tn=0.8 MeV. This is relatively close to the mass-deficit Δ⁢m, so the dominant term here is the exponential (as mn/mp≃1). At freeze-out this ratio is therefore

NnNp=(mnmp)3/2⁢exp⁡(-Δ⁢m⁢c2kB⁢Tn)≃0.20 (17)

From this point onwards converting protons to neutrons is energetically impossible, so the only process which can change this ratio is the decay of free neutrons. Forming helium (and heavier elements) requires both neutrons and protons, while hydrogen (1H) requires only protons, so the neutron abundance sets an upper limit on how much helium can be formed. An 24He nucleus consists of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so if we assume that all the neutrons are used to form helium then NHe=Nn/2. The mass of a helium-4 nucleus is 4 times the neutron mass, so the mass fraction666 Stellar astronomers use X to denote the mass fraction of hydrogen, then Y for helium, and Z for all the heavier elements (“metals”) combined. Here we also wish to distinguish between the different isotopes of the light elements, so the mass fraction of helium-4 is usually denoted by Y4. of 24He is

Y4=4⁢NHeNp+Nn=2⁢NnNp+Nn=2NpNn+1 (18)

Substituting in the value Np/Nn≃5.0 from Equation 17, we find an upper limit Y4,max≤0.33. This is slightly larger than the present-day observed value, so it’s plausible that all the helium in the Universe was formed during the big bang.

An accurate estimate of Y4 (the “primordial” abundance of helium) further requires us to consider the effect of neutron decay. After proton/neutron freeze-out, the formation of heavier elements proceeds by essentially the same chain of nuclear reactions that drive fusion in the cores of stars. These reactions also proceed in both forward and reverse directions until the temperature drops sufficiently, and here freeze-out happens at kB⁢THe=0.06 MeV. We use Equation 14 to find the age corresponding to this temperature:

tHe=1⁢s⁢(1.1⁢MeVkB⁢THe)2≃340⁢s (19)

This is comparable to the neutron half-life, so we expect a significant fraction of the neutrons to have decayed into protons before forming helium. The neutron-to-proton density ratio (Equation 17) therefore becomes777 This approach only “counts” the decrease in the number of neutrons, whereas strictly we should also consider the corresponding increase in the number of protons. However, because protons are already much more abundant this is a negligible correction.

NnNp=(mnmp)3/2⁢exp⁡(-Δ⁢m⁢c2kB⁢Tn)×exp⁡(-tHetn)≃0.14 (20)

and, substituting into Equation 18 we find

Y4≃0.24 (21)

This is almost exactly the helium abundance that is observed in all sorts of astronomical objects (stars, gas clouds, distant galaxies, etc.).

Similar calculations (with more complex reaction chains) yield corresponding predictions for the abundances of 12H (deuterium), 23He and 37Li, which turn out to be ≃10-4, 10-5, and 10-10, respectively. All of these can be measured directly (by taking spectra of stars, gas clouds, galaxies, etc.), and the predictions of primordial nucleosynthesis therefore provide one of the most powerful tests of the hot big bang model.

Finally, these observations also yield a very tight constraint on the total baryonic mass in the Universe888 Within the context of the ΛCDM model (which makes some additional assumptions), CMB observations set an even tighter constraint on Ωb.

0.021≤Ωb⁢h2≤0.025 (22)

Thus baryons account for approximately 4% of the critical density, confirming our earlier assertion that most of the observed matter in the Universe must be non-baryonic.
